intro: A rocking left hand supports a melody that repeatedly grows a second voice. Listen for the difference between the notes that carry the phrase and the ornaments that delay their arrival.
question: How does a returning melody change without losing its shape?

CENS diagonal mean 0.949, sustained 16.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 204 s (cache/form/chopin-nocturne-op27-2.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). cues.title: Singing above broken chords
cues.text: Across the opening, broken chords support a slower singing line. Chopin marks the piece “Lento sostenuto” — slow and sustained. Listen for how the melody connects notes whose piano sound begins decaying as soon as they are struck.
cues.evidence: The score specifies this opening texture and marking. The report places a relatively quiet D♭-centred span at the start; individual notes are not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One voice and two
cues.text: The nocturne repeatedly lets its melody grow into paired voices, often in thirds and sixths. When that happens, follow the lower melodic note as well as the top one: the duet is part of the phrase, not just added weight.
cues.evidence: The paired writing is a score feature described in John Henken’s LA Phil note. The change around 0:42 suggests an expanding phrase, but does not locate a particular doubling.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The phrase gathers activity
cues.text: In this stretch, the phrase becomes more active before drawing back. Try to keep hold of the longer melodic line through the quicker notes around it.
cues.evidence: The report shows rising relative level and more attacks around 0:50–1:10, followed by a retreat around 1:15–1:20. This is a passage-level contour.

cues.title: A Parisian dedication
cues.text: The two Op. 27 Nocturnes were published in 1836 and dedicated to Countess Thérèse d’Apponyi, whose Paris salon Chopin frequented. The dedication identifies a patron, not a hidden subject for the music.
cues.evidence: John Henken’s LA Phil programme note documents publication and dedication: https://www.laphil.com/works/two-nocturnes-op-27

cues.title: A decorated return
cues.text: The opening melody returns more than once in this nocturne. Around each return, compare the familiar phrase with its changing ornaments and the expansion that follows; the design is not simply quiet–stormy–quiet.
cues.evidence: Henken describes three strophes beginning with the same melody. A quieter tonic-centred span around 1:55–2:10 supports the first return’s approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep the longer line
cues.text: The more forceful writing in this stretch still belongs to a melodic phrase. Listen beyond the quicker notes for the points where the line leans on a harmony and where it releases that pressure.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises across 2:30–2:55 and remains high through much of 3:00–3:20. The report does not identify individual ornaments or voices.

cues.title: The melody returns again
cues.text: In this later return, compare the familiar melody with its earlier versions. Ornament changes what the phrase contains without requiring a wholly new tune.
cues.evidence: A strong measured change around 3:26 and a quieter D♭-centred span through 3:45 are compatible with the score’s third strophe. The return time remains an estimate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another broad swell
cues.text: The later expansion rises towards another crest. Follow the length of the phrase through the decorative movement rather than treating every quick note as a separate destination.
cues.evidence: The report’s highest five-second relative-level window is around 4:25, after a rise beginning around 4:05. The cue concerns that build, not a single climax note.

cues.title: The coda stays close
cues.text: The closing span stays near D♭ while small changes continue within the texture. Listen for how the accompaniment can move without requiring the whole phrase to leave its tonal centre.
cues.evidence: The score’s coda follows the final expansion. Lower recorded level after 4:35 and a persistent low D♭ through much of the remaining minute support this approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chopin plays in Leipzig
cues.text: Chopin played this nocturne during his September 1835 visit to Leipzig, where he met Schumann and Mendelssohn at Friedrich Wieck’s house. Mendelssohn later told his sister Fanny that he had learnt a substantial part of the new piece by ear.
cues.evidence: Henken’s LA Phil programme note identifies the visit, the work and Mendelssohn’s letter: https://www.laphil.com/works/two-nocturnes-op-27

cues.title: Listen past the attack
cues.text: Through the closing phrases, listen to the sound left after each attack. The remaining resonance contributes to the ending even as fresh notes become less frequent.
cues.evidence: The analysis records fewer attacks around 5:40–6:00 and a long fall in level through 6:15. It cannot determine the pianist’s pedalling or a precise final release.

transitions.title: The melody acquires a lower voice
transitions.how: The first D♭ major phrase settles, but the left hand keeps its six-note broken-chord motion. The continuation turns towards B♭ minor, the relative minor, while the right hand thickens into paired voices. Thirds and sixths make the lower melodic strand audible alongside the top note; the bass changes the harmony beneath a recognisable accompanimental pattern. This is an expansion within the same slow 6/8, not a separately paced middle section.
transitions.evidence: The expansion boundary is 0:42, also an analysis boundary; level and brightness rise afterwards, with B♭-minor estimates around 0:45–0:50. The score supplies the relative-minor continuation, paired right-hand voices and unchanged accompaniment. John Henken describes the strophic rather than ternary design: https://www.laphil.com/works/two-nocturnes-op-27. Individual doublings are not timed.

transitions.title: A dominant clears the decorated line
transitions.how: The expansion’s chromatic harmony is gathered back onto A♭, the dominant of D♭. Its resolution restores D♭ in the bass and the opening singing line above the familiar broken chords. The texture becomes less crowded before ornament begins enriching the melody again. Listen for the bass arrival rather than a halt in the accompaniment: Chopin makes the returning phrase sound like a renewed breath within continuing motion.
transitions.evidence: The first-return marker is 1:56, a measured boundary. Analysis shows A♭ in the bass around 1:50 and a quiet D♭-centred region at 1:55–2:10. The score supplies the dominant–tonic return and opening melody; the provisional relation matches 1:58–2:21.5 to an opening phrase. Pitch estimates support the location, not the chord identification.

transitions.title: The tonic pitch turns minor
transitions.how: The second expansion darkens the tonic itself: D♭ is respelt C♯, and major gives way to C♯ minor. The melody becomes more densely voiced and more urgent, but the left hand retains its broken-chord current. Because the tonic pitch survives the change of spelling and mode, the departure feels closer than a move to an unrelated key. Chromatic movement in the inner notes then loosens that temporary foothold and drives the wider expansion.
transitions.evidence: The darker-expansion boundary is 2:34, one of the stronger measured changes. Relative level rises after 2:30 and the estimates move into a C♯-minor region. The score supplies the enharmonic tonic-minor writing and continuing broken-chord accompaniment; the analysis is not used to generate harmonic labels. This is an approximate phrase location.

transitions.title: The bass arrives before ornament settles
transitions.how: The forceful expansion presses towards A♭ dominant harmony, then releases into D♭ major and the opening melody. Bass and accompaniment recover the original tonal foundation while the right hand continues the process of decoration. The contrast lies in harmonic arrival and a thinning of texture, not a new tempo: the same rocking subdivision links the expansive passage to the more exposed song. Its familiar contour remains audible beneath the altered surface.
transitions.evidence: The second-return marker is 3:26, the report’s strongest boundary. The 3:20 window is A♭-based; D♭ is established by 3:25 as brightness falls. The score supplies the dominant resolution and third strophe; the provisional relation matches 3:27–3:43.5 with the opening. The join is not note-aligned.

transitions.title: The bass stops travelling
transitions.how: The last expansion relaxes through A♭ dominant harmony into a D♭ bass that the coda repeatedly renews. Above this tonic pedal, the right hand can continue its duet and chromatic inflections without starting another tonal departure. The left hand’s moving notes now prolong a place rather than lead to a new one. Later rising sixths extend the upper register while the bass keeps the conclusion grounded in D♭ major.
transitions.evidence: The coda boundary is 4:40, also a measured change after the 4:25 crest. Analysis shows A♭-centred windows at 4:30–4:35 and persistent low D♭ thereafter. The written coda supplies the tonic pedal and closing duet in sixths; Henken also identifies the latter: https://www.laphil.com/works/two-nocturnes-op-27. The later sixths are not assigned an entrance time.

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
